source: Dr. Thaveesak Sangudom, Dr. Theerawut Chutinanthakun, and Wirot Horasart, "Off-season Production Techniques for Pursat Orange (ក្រូចពោធិ៍សាត់ / kroch poursat) in Cambodia," in The Guideline of Climate Change Adaptation in Cambodia (pp. 130-153), Project on Promoting Climate Resilience in Farming Communities of Cambodia, General Department of Agriculture (GDA) Cambodia, Thailand International Cooperation Agency (TICA), and Department of Agriculture (DOA) Thailand, 2017-2020.
text:
The source reports a direct income comparison between the demonstration orchard (using the off-season techniques described in this batch) and five other farmers growing Pursat orange with traditional methods, all in the same area, for a single season:

- Demonstration orchard (Roeurm Sokha): 49 trees, total income 3,000,000 riel
- Farmer 2 (Li Chamroeun): 40 trees, total income 750,000 riel
- Farmer 3 (Lim Sokunthea): 60 trees, total income 1,700,000 riel
- Farmer 4 (Mem Sokha): 49 trees, total income 900,000 riel
- Farmer 5 (Nuon Norry): 50 trees, total income 1,000,000 riel
- Farmer 6 (Kiem Suyon): 50 trees, total income 1,090,000 riel

The demonstration orchard and Farmer 4 had the same number of trees (49), which gives the cleanest like-for-like comparison: 3,000,000 riel versus 900,000 riel, a roughly 3.3-fold difference. This matches the source's own separate summary statement that adopting farmers received more than three times the income of farmers using traditional methods with a similar number of trees. The source attributes this gain to the combination of off-season timing (capturing higher prices when supply is otherwise low), the higher sugar-content/quality standard achieved (see harvest quality entry), and the more precise irrigation and fertilizer program described elsewhere in this batch.
